name: Hydrolyzed hyaluronic acid
lead: Hydrolyzed hyaluronic acid is hyaluronic acid (HA) that has been broken into shorter chains, and it is marketed in skincare serums and moisturizers as a low-molecular-weight form meant to hydrate deeper than standard HA. People use it to make skin look plumper, smoother and more hydrated, since HA is a glycosaminoglycan found in skin and other connective tissues that binds water and supports hydration [1].

Chain length matters biologically: high-molecular-weight HA and low-molecular-weight fragments behave differently in cell studies, and some very small fragments have been reported to promote angiogenesis and inflammatory responses [1][2][6]. Reference coverage of HA does not address how well topically applied hydrolyzed HA penetrates skin [1], but laboratory work has reported that HA fragments of about 5 and 8 kDa passed through the outer skin layer while larger HA stayed on the surface [7].

In a small randomized trial in older adults with dry skin, a lotion containing low-molecular-weight HA raised skin hydration readings more than a high-molecular-weight HA lotion or the vehicle after four weeks [8]. Other human evidence on hydrolyzed HA as a topical ingredient comes from studies of multi-ingredient products.

paras: In vivo, HA polymers range from about 5,000 to 20,000,000 daltons; synovial HA averages around 7 MDa, and a 70 kg person has roughly 15 g of HA, about a third of which turns over each day [1]. Acid or alkaline hydrolysis, ultrasound, heat and oxidants can degrade HA into smaller pieces [1]. Cosmetic products list the shortened forms as hydrolyzed hyaluronic acid.
HA used in products and fillers comes from animal sources such as rooster combs, from microbial fermentation, or from chemical synthesis; Bacillus subtilis has been engineered to produce it [1].

Karl Meyer and John Palmer first isolated hyaluronic acid in 1934 from bovine vitreous [1]. A 1953 paper in Science examined a diffusible component of hydrolyzed HA in relation to vaccinia virus inactivation [3]. A 1985 Science paper reported that HA degradation products induced angiogenesis [2]. Pharmacia's Healon, developed in the 1970s and 1980s, brought HA into eye surgery, and HA later became a common skin care ingredient and dermal filler material [1].

In cell studies summarised in encyclopedia coverage, HA above about 500 kDa stimulated HA synthesis in cultured synovial fibroblasts, while low-molecular-weight HA at high concentrations inhibited it [1]. Degradation fragments have been reported to trigger inflammatory responses in immune cells [1]. A review of HA in wound healing summarizes that high-molecular-weight HA displays anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive properties, whereas low-molecular-weight HA is a potent proinflammatory molecule in those settings [6].

A consensus paper on late-onset reactions to HA dermal fillers lists the physicochemical structure of the filler, particularly low-molecular-weight HA, as one of three hypotheses for how rare delayed reactions arise; it concerns injected fillers, not topical products [9].

Proponents say short chains can slip between the cells of the stratum corneum and hold water where long chains remain on the surface as a film. An in vitro penetration study reported that HA of 5 and 8 kDa crossed the stratum corneum and entered the epidermis and dermis, whereas higher-molecular-weight HA was trapped on the surface; the same work found low-molecular-weight HA interacted with keratin and lipids in the skin barrier and had a substantial hydrating effect [7].

Hydrolyzed HA is promoted in serums as a smaller molecule meant to reach deeper than standard HA, and it is often listed alongside other humectants and peptides in hydrating routines. Formulas typically layer it under a moisturizer.

A double-blind randomized trial in 36 nursing-home residents aged 60 to 80 in Jakarta with dry skin applied three lotions (low-molecular-weight HA, high-molecular-weight HA, or vehicle) to three separate leg sites. After four weeks, the low-molecular-weight HA site showed higher skin capacitance than the high-molecular-weight HA site (56.37 vs 52.37 AU, p = 0.004) and vehicle (56.37 vs 49.01 AU, p < 0.001); transepidermal water loss and symptom scores did not differ between groups, and no side effects were found [8].

One preprint reported a face serum combining bakuchiol, palmitoyl tripeptide-38, hydrolyzed HA and a polyherbal and vitamin blend; it was tested in vitro, in a patch test in 55 healthy adults (no irritation or allergic contact dermatitis reported) and in a human efficacy trial, with the authors reporting improved skin quality [4]. Because the product had many ingredients, the contribution of hydrolyzed HA cannot be separated.

Injected products that mix high and low molecular weight HA have also been studied, including a 2025 clinical trial of a hybrid-complex injection for face rejuvenation [10]. Lab work has used hydrolyzed HA gels to make microneedles [5].

card.summary: Chopped-up hyaluronic acid sold as the deeper-penetrating hydrator; direct evidence is thin.
card.note: No standalone topical trials; very small HA fragments have shown pro-inflammatory activity in cell studies.

quick.overview:
Hydrolyzed hyaluronic acid is hyaluronic acid broken into shorter chains. Brands market it as getting deeper into skin than regular HA.

The only human data found come from a multi-ingredient serum, so its own effect has not been isolated.
quick.mechanism: HA binds water and supports skin hydration; shorter chains are argued to reach further, though encyclopedia coverage does not address topical penetration.
quick.risks: A patch test of a serum containing it reported no irritation or allergy in 55 adults. Laboratory work shows small HA fragments can provoke inflammatory responses in cells.

chain: Binds water and may reach deeper layers of the outer skin
Skin looks more hydrated and plump
angle.text: Users apply serums and moisturizers containing hydrolyzed HA to dry or dull skin to make it look and feel more hydrated. In the one randomized trial that compared molecular weights, low-molecular-weight HA raised skin hydration measurements more than high-molecular-weight HA.
